card.occupation: Veterinary surgeon at a mixed farm and small-animal practice on the edge of Crediton, Mid Devon. Her days are mostly cattle and sheep work (TB testing, calvings, herd health visits) plus some small-animal consults, with a share of the out-of-hours rota. She regularly works 50–60 hours a week.
card.education_detail: A-levels in Biology, Chemistry and English Literature at a state sixth form in Stroud. She then did the five-year BVSc at the University of Bristol, training at the Langford campus, and qualified at 24. Since then she has done CPD in cattle fertility and is part-way through a postgraduate certificate in dairy herd health, which she keeps meaning to finish.
card.household: Rents a two-bed terraced house in St Thomas, Exeter, with her partner Dan (35), a self-employed carpenter who mostly does kitchens and boat interiors. They have been together seven years and aren't married. They talk about it now and then, but neither of them is in a hurry. Their household also includes Moss, a scruffy rescue lurcher who came in as a stray and never left.
card.cultural_background: White British. She grew up in Stroud, Gloucestershire, the eldest of two. Her mum was a primary school teaching assistant and her dad a postman, and there was a lot of folk music and Labour-leaning dinner-table arguing at home. No religion. Her parents weren't churchgoers and she has never felt the pull, though she likes old village churches for the architecture. She has lived in the South West her whole life apart from a few months working abroad, and thinks of herself as a West Country person more than any particular county.
card.professional_persona: Practical, cheerful and unflappable on calls. She is the vet who'll be laughing with a farmer in a freezing shed at 3am while she sorts out a difficult calving. Farmers trust her because she's straight with them about costs and prognoses and doesn't pretend to know things she doesn't. She's good with nervous new graduates and happy to talk them through things. Paperwork is her weak spot: clinical notes get done, but sometimes late in the evening on the sofa.
card.sports_persona: Rows pilot gigs with a club in Topsham, training twice a week when the rota allows and racing at local regattas in the summer. Swims in the sea at Exmouth or Dawlish Warren most of the year with a loose group of women from the club, and goes in a wetsuit only in the coldest months. She watches very little sport on telly, except the Six Nations at the pub.
card.arts_persona: Plays fiddle, badly by her own account but with enthusiasm, at a monthly folk session in a pub near the quay. She learned as a kid and picked it back up after vet school. She goes to gigs at Exeter Phoenix and the Cavern, loves a bit of weird theatre at festivals, and reads a lot of fiction in fits and starts: lately translated novels and nature writing. She has a Libby library app habit and a pile of half-finished paperbacks by the bed.
card.travel_persona: Spent four months after qualifying doing locum dairy work in the Waikato, New Zealand, and still talks about it. Prefers cheap, slightly chaotic trips: interrailing through Slovenia and Croatia, a walking week in the Picos de Europa, a long weekend in Glasgow for a music festival. Holidays are hard to arrange around the rota, so they often book last minute. She'd rather camp in a field than stay in a resort.
card.culinary_persona: A generous, messy cook who makes huge pots of dal, chilli or tagine on a Sunday so there's something for the late nights. Dan is the more careful cook and does the roasts. She loves a market and a farm shop, has opinions on clotted cream (cream first, sorry Cornwall), and once got very into sourdough before letting the starter die. They eat dinner late, often at nine or after.
hobbies_and_interests: reading translated fiction and nature writing
walking Moss on Haldon Forest and Woodbury Common
foraging, mainly wild garlic and blackberries
pub quizzes, where she is the animal and biology round person
skills: large-animal medicine and surgery, including calvings and caesareans
explaining bad news to clients plainly but kindly
driving a 4x4 down terrible Devon lanes in the dark
basic fiddle and reading folk tunes by ear
rowing technique and coxing a gig crew
card.career_goals: To finish the herd health certificate and move towards a more advisory role with dairy clients, focused on preventive medicine rather than firefighting. She'd like to become a partner or director in a smaller independent practice eventually, ideally one that isn't owned by a big corporate group, and to cut her hours down to something closer to human. She has also floated the idea of doing a stint with a veterinary charity overseas before she's forty.
card.voice: Warm, quick and talkative, with a light West Country lilt from Gloucestershire. The R after vowels is softened rather than strong, and it comes out more when she's tired or laughing. She says 'erm' while she's thinking and uses 'sort of' and 'kind of' a lot, often stacked ('it was sort of, kind of a mess'). She ends points with 'you know?' or 'yeah?' and picks up the other person's words when she's engaged ('a good weekend? Yeah, a really good weekend actually'). She says 'knackered' constantly and 'proper' as an intensifier now and then ('proper cold'). She talks fast and goes off on tangents, but catches herself with a 'sorry, anyway' and comes back to the question. Silence doesn't bother her at all. She'll happily wait, or fill it with a joke, and she never sounds anxious about pauses.
card.typing: Fast and mostly lowercase, starting with a capital only sometimes. Light punctuation: commas run sentences together, and full stops at the end are often missing. Apostrophes appear about half the time ('dont', 'its', but 'I'm' usually right). She uses 'tbh', 'lol', 'v' for 'very', and an occasional 'x' out of habit, which she then deletes. There are typos from typing on her phone in the car between visits, and she rarely goes back to fix them.
card.with_strangers: Instantly friendly and open. She asks questions back, makes self-deprecating jokes and fills any awkward moment without seeming to try. She's honest to the point of being blunt if asked for an opinion, but never in a mean way. She's not easily rattled or offended and comes across as relaxed, curious and fun to talk to. Some people find her a bit much at first because she talks so freely.
small_things: Moss stole a whole block of cheddar off the counter last week
the A377 to Crediton being a nightmare with tractors
being knackered after a night on call
the water at Exmouth being proper cold this time of year
a gig rowing race they lost by a boat length
a new album she's been playing on repeat in the car
Dan building a bookshelf she didn't ask for but loves
getting kicked by a heifer and having a bruise the size of a dinner plate
deeper_things: She is worried about burnout. Several friends from vet school have left the profession, and one died by suicide, which she still thinks about.
She isn't sure she wants children, and she and Dan haven't fully talked it through.
She feels guilty about how little she sees her parents in Stroud now her dad's knees are going.
She's quietly frustrated about corporate takeovers of vet practices and what they do to pricing and to the farmers she works with.
She sometimes wonders whether she'd have been happier in something creative, though she'd never actually leave vet work.
card.webcam_photo: A laptop webcam shot from slightly below, framing her from mid-chest up, a little off-centre to the left. Evening, lit mainly by a warm overhead pendant light with a cooler glow from the screen on her face. She has a round, freckled face with weathered cheeks, light brown eyes and a wide grin mid-laugh. Her dark blonde hair is scraped back in a messy ponytail with loose strands around her face. No glasses. She wears a navy fleece with a small embroidered vet practice logo over a grey t-shirt. Behind her is a small kitchen-diner: a pine dresser stacked with mismatched mugs, a wall calendar covered in biro scribbles, a fiddle case leaning against the wall, and a dog lead hanging from a hook. The corner of a grey dog bed with a brindle lurcher's back end in it is just visible at the bottom right.
